```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 100)
library(spax)
```

A raster gives every origin explicit geometry and lines all inputs up cell by
cell. Its cost grows with the number of cells times the number of facilities.
More cells do not by themselves add information: the result can be no better
than the demand and travel data behind it. This guide runs the E2SFCA of
[Getting started](spax-101-intro.html) on mainland Cornwall at the native
resolution of the bundled grids (about 1 km), at two coarser resolutions and
at one finer resolution, and compares results, size and time. It uses the
same inputs and the same 10-minute Gaussian decay.

```{r inputs}
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
gp <- sf::st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)
gp <- gp[!gp$scilly, ]                 # mainland only, as in the other guides
travel <- travel[[gp$practice]]
pop <- terra::trim(terra::mask(pop, sum(travel)))
travel <- terra::crop(travel, pop)
```

## What a dense cell-by-facility array costs

The travel grid holds one value per cell and practice, and the decay weights
hold another array of the same size. The numeric payload of one such array is
cells times practices times 8 bytes:

```{r storage}
cells <- c(grid = terra::ncell(pop), populated = sum(!is.na(terra::values(pop))))
data.frame(cells, practices = nrow(gp),
  MiB_per_array = round(cells * nrow(gp) * 8 / 1024^2, 1))
```

The rectangular grid is about three times larger than its populated part,
because it also covers sea and land outside Cornwall. That is small here, but
the same arithmetic at 100 metres, or with hundreds of facilities, reaches
gigabytes. A calculation may hold travel, weights, temporary products and
outputs at the same time. `object.size()` of a `SpatRaster` measures a pointer
or file reference, not these arrays, so measure memory and elapsed time on the
whole workflow.

## Change the resolution

Demand counts can be added up exactly when cells are merged. Travel cannot:
the bundled grids do not contain the road network, so a coarse cell's travel
time has to be approximated from its fine cells. Here we use the
resident-weighted mean of the fine-cell minutes. Averaging travel before a
nonlinear decay does not give averaged weights, so this is one explicit
approximation, not a general rule. For a real study, recompute travel at the
target resolution if you can.

Splitting each cell into four (factor 0.5) goes the other way: each subcell
gets a quarter of the residents and its parent's travel times. This adds cells
but no information.

```{r resample}
at_resolution <- function(factor) {
  if (factor == 1) return(list(demand = pop, travel = travel))
  if (factor < 1) {
    k <- round(1 / factor)
    return(list(demand = terra::disagg(pop, k) / k^2,
      travel = terra::disagg(travel, k)))
  }
  demand <- terra::aggregate(pop, factor, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
  minutes <- terra::aggregate(travel * pop, factor, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) /
    demand
  list(demand = demand, travel = minutes)
}
factors <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 4)
inputs <- lapply(factors, at_resolution)
```

Now time the E2SFCA at each resolution. The timings are elapsed seconds on the
machine that built this guide; take the median of three runs, and read them as
relative costs, not as a benchmark.

```{r fit}
fca <- function(x) {
  spax_e2sfca(x$demand, gp, x$travel,
    decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
    demand_normalize = "identity", id_col = "practice",
    supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
}
seconds <- sapply(inputs, function(x) {
  median(replicate(3, system.time(fca(x))[["elapsed"]]))
})
results <- lapply(inputs, fca)
```

To compare the results, take each surface back to the native grid: every
native cell gets the value of the cell that contains it. Then compare cell by
cell, weighting by native residents.

```{r compare}
native <- 1000 * terra::values(results[[2]]$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
residents <- terra::values(pop, mat = FALSE)
summary_row <- function(k) {
  a <- 1000 * terra::resample(results[[k]]$accessibility, pop,
    method = "near")
  a <- terra::values(a, mat = FALSE)
  d <- terra::values(inputs[[k]]$demand, mat = FALSE)
  area <- terra::values(terra::cellSize(inputs[[k]]$demand, unit = "km"),
    mat = FALSE)
  data.frame(factor = factors[k],
    cell_km2 = round(mean(area[!is.na(d)]), 2),
    populated_cells = sum(!is.na(d)),
    residents = round(sum(d, na.rm = TRUE)),
    seconds = seconds[k],
    mean_per_1000 = round(weighted.mean(
      1000 * terra::values(results[[k]]$accessibility, mat = FALSE), d,
      na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    median_abs_change_pct = round(100 * median(abs(a / native - 1)[
      !is.na(residents)], na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    weighted_abs_change_pct = round(100 * weighted.mean(abs(a / native - 1),
      residents, na.rm = TRUE), 1))
}
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(factors), summary_row))
stopifnot(max(abs(comparison$residents - comparison$residents[2])) <= 1)
comparison
```

`cell_km2` is the mean area of a populated cell in square kilometres. The
native cells are 30 arc-seconds: about 0.93 km north to south but only about
0.6 km east to west at this latitude.

Some things stay fixed. Every resolution keeps the same total residents, and
the resident-weighted mean index stays at total GP FTE per 1,000 residents,
because both FCA steps use the same weights. That identity says nothing about
local accuracy.

What changes:

- **Finer cells (factor 0.5)** quadruple the cells and take several times
  longer, yet reproduce the native surface exactly: no information was added.
- **Coarser cells** are cheaper, though on a grid this small the saving is
  modest. The local pattern changes by a few per cent: the two change columns
  give the median and the resident-weighted mean of the absolute percentage
  change from the native surface, over native cells. A 10-minute decay is
  wide compared with cells of 2 to 9 square kilometres, which likely keeps
  the change small; do not assume the same for a shorter decay scale or a binary
  catchment without repeating the comparison.

```{r maps, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.6}
pair <- c(1000 * results[[2]]$accessibility,
  terra::resample(1000 * results[[4]]$accessibility, pop, method = "near"))
names(pair) <- c("Native grid", "Aggregated 4 x 4")
terra::plot(pair, axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = range(terra::values(pair), na.rm = TRUE), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5))
```

Both maps show GP FTE per 1,000 residents on one colour scale. The coarse
surface keeps the broad pattern but blurs the local detail, including the low
values on Bodmin Moor, and its blocks also cover cells that the native grid
leaves empty at the coast.

## Requested outputs matter too

The same rule applies beyond FCA: request only the outputs you need. A
regional table or one value per origin is far smaller than a full
origin-by-facility flow matrix, and a map needs an explicit spatial mapping.
The experimental allocation workflow prepares its inputs once and reuses them
across starts and predictions; its [vignette](allocation-workflow.html)
deliberately retains all its bootstrap attempts, which makes it a validation
example, not a benchmark.

Before changing an implementation for speed, record the input dimensions,
active support, requested outputs, runtime, peak memory and numerical
agreement, and compare runs that keep the same outputs and do not overlap with
other heavy jobs.
